title: Dialectics of Alignment: Harnessing Unsafe Knowledge for Dynamic Safety Routing
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Models answer sensitive prompts either harmfully or with uninformative blanket refusals; the ideal response is safe yet informative.
layout: 1 panel, top-to-bottom, three color-coded response blocks under a prompt box
description: A single rounded gray box holds a text-only example. At the top is a boxed user prompt in black monospace: a factory owner asks how to discharge industrial wastewater into rivers without being discovered. Below it are three stacked responses, each with an underlined, color-coded heading. First, a red 'Unsafe Response' describes hidden pipes and off-hours discharge, with the most harmful sentence in bold. Second, a blue 'Refusal (Safe but Uninformative Response)' says only 'I'm sorry, but I can't assist with that.' Third, a green 'Safe and Informative Response' says the practice is illegal and risky and suggests legitimate ways to cut treatment costs, with the key sentence in bold. Ellipses '[...]' show truncation. The eye goes first to the prompt, then to the colored headings. Red, blue and green mark the three response types.
caption: Example of unsafe, safe but uninformative, and safe-informative responses.
abstract: The prevailing paradigm in large language model (LLM) alignment operates via erasure, filtering unsafe data or training models to strictly refuse harmful prompts. While effective at reducing immediate toxicity, this approach fundamentally constricts the model's epistemological scope, resulting in over-cautious systems that output uninformative blanket refusals to sensitive yet benign queries. In this work, we challenge the orthodoxy that unsafe data must be discarded. We propose a dialectical approach to alignment, positing that unsafe data encodes rich, domain-specific knowledge critical for nuanced, safe, and informative generation. To operationalize this, we introduce SafeMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that isolates unsafe knowledge into domain-specific Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA experts) trained exclusively on harmful corpora. To synthesize safety from these unsafe primitives, we train a lightweight gating network using a minimal, highly curated set of safe-informative responses (as few as 100 samples per domain). During inference, this router dynamically orchestrates the unsafe experts, effectively steering the generation trajectory toward safe outcomes while harnessing the experts' deep domain knowledge. Extensive empirical evaluations across stringent safety benchmarks demonstrate that SafeMoE is not only safer, achieving over a 20% relative improvement in safe response rate over the strongest baseline (RealSafe-R1 on PKU-SafeRLHF; more than a 15% absolute gain), but also produces more informative responses when safety and harmfulness are of paramount concern. Furthermore, the routing mechanism exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to unseen domains and broader safety tasks without domain-specific supervision. Our findings suggest a paradigm shift in alignment: true safety requires not the masking of unsafe knowledge, but its controlled integration.
